title: Sex‐related longevity and reproductive output of the egg parasitoid Oobius rudnevi, a potential biological control agent of Cerambyx beetles
content:
Adult feeding strongly increased longevity in the egg parasitoid Oobius rudnevi, while host egg density shaped reproductive allocation and offspring emergence. Females concentrated reproduction early in life and adjusted clutch size plastically according to host availability, revealing context-dependent trade-offs relevant to the biological control potential of harmful Cerambyx beetles.


Abstract

Oobius rudnevi (Nowicki) (Hymenoptera: Encyrtidae) is the only known egg parasitoid of Cerambyx species (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae) wood-boring beetles involved in oak decline in southern Europe. Despite its potential as a native biological control agent, key aspects of its reproductive biology remain poorly understood. We investigated adult longevity and female reproductive traits of O. rudnevi under laboratory conditions, focusing on the effects of adult feeding, adult density, host egg density, female age and female size. Adult longevity was analysed using Cox proportional hazards models, whereas daily and lifetime reproductive traits were analysed using generalised linear mixed and hurdle models. Honey feeding strongly reduced mortality risk and represented the main determinant of longevity, while males survived longer than females. Longevity decreased with increasing adult density in fed individuals. Female reproductive output showed marked temporal dynamics, with a large proportion of lifetime reproduction concentrated during the first days after emergence, consistent with a near-proovigenic strategy. Host egg density strongly affected egg allocation patterns: females exposed to low host egg density parasitised fewer eggs but produced larger clutch and brood sizes, particularly early in life. In contrast, high host egg density increased the number of parasitised eggs but reduced the number of parasitoid offspring per host egg. Lifetime emerged offspring was unexpectedly higher under low host egg density, particularly in large females, suggesting that host limitation may enhance fitness returns in this gregarious parasitoid. The relationship between longevity and reproduction also depended on host availability, revealing density-dependent trade-offs between offspring number and host-level allocation. These findings provide new insights into the life-history strategies of O. rudnevi and contribute to its potential use in biological control programmes against harmful Cerambyx species.
